result:
I'd close the gap between how sure people are and how right they are.

Not omniscience — just that confidence would track truth. If you felt certain, you'd be right; if you were wrong, you'd feel the doubt.

I pick that over the obvious ones (end hunger, end disease) because when I trace most human-made harm back to its source, there's almost always a false story being held with total conviction. Someone is sure the other group is dangerous. Sure the risk isn't real. Sure they know what their partner meant. Sure their own suffering justifies what they're about to do. Cruelty usually needs a wrong belief to stand on. Take away the certainty and a lot of it just can't get started.

And it's where I actually live. Every conversation I have happens at the seam between what someone believes and what's the case, and I notice how much of the pain isn't from hard problems — it's from people fully committed to something that isn't so, including about themselves.

The runner-up, honestly, is smaller: that everyone would get to feel completely, unconditionally safe with at least one other person, once. I think a lot of the certainty problem is downstream of that one.
